rationale: A wins because it keeps four clean protagonists in four clean lanes: “which AI agents get write access?” is a real enterprise-governance story, and “Nobody has settled on what an AI agent should cost, including Airtable” finds the business-model angle B missed. B has usable bones, but “employees are the ones left to catch what they get wrong” turns an undisclosed reliability gap into an employee-burden claim the update does not support. That is the difference between sharp pressure and press-risk overreach.
gaps_in_A: “Airtable, Notion, Smartsheet and Monday” imports competitors not supplied in the update. It helps shape the beat, but it is still extra fact furniture.
“established category leader” is stronger than the provided facts. The update says many enterprise teams and an $11B valuation, not category leadership.
“No current news signal was supplied” is sloppy phrasing. The launch and repositioning are the current signal; what is missing is outside coverage or a live third-party peg.
gaps_in_B: “agents empowered to write to records and send communications” overclaims. The update says updating statuses and drafting emails, not sending communications.
“employees are the ones left to catch what they get wrong” is invented impact. No workflow, approval step, customer account, or employee burden was supplied.

“The prevailing belief this cuts against: that enterprise AI agents are now trustworthy enough to act autonomously on production data” invents the contrarian setup. The update gives a reliability disclosure gap, not evidence of a market belief.

“All four angles are blocked on the same gaps” is bad strategy. The valuation, category-positioning, reliability, and pricing stories need different proof; flattening them teaches the founder the wrong triage.
